questions.stem: Identify the four problems a factory of 2,000 strangers faced in 1910.
options: Communication, coordination, motivation, and productivity and quality
Taxes, labour laws, customers and suppliers
Hybrid work, AI, globalisation and sustainability
Pay, offices, job titles and holiday entitlements
questions.why: Each of these problems produced a school of management thinking. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Describe the chapter's view of management ideas.
options: Each idea is an answer to a real workplace problem of its time
Ideas are invented by professors mainly so that students can be examined on them
Old ideas are always wrong and should be replaced as soon as a newer idea appears
New ideas always replace old ones completely, so only the latest wave matters today
questions.why: Ideas are answers to problems; that is why they evolved. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Explain why bigger firms needed new management thinking.
options: Instructions, roles and motivation that worked for 40 known workers broke with 2,000 strangers
Bigger firms had more money to spend on consultants, who sold them new ideas
Workers in big firms were less skilled than those in small workshops and needed more rules
Governments forced big firms to change their methods through new factory legislation
questions.why: Growth broke the old informal way of managing. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Identify the main focus of the human relations wave.
options: People and their feelings at work
Efficiency and the one best way of doing each job
Flexibility, systems and reading the situation
Rules and hierarchy
questions.why: The 1930s wave put people first after Hawthorne. See §2.2.

questions.stem: Identify the approximate decade when each wave began.
options: Classical ~1900s, human relations ~1930s, modern ~1950s onward
Classical ~1950s, human relations ~1900s, modern ~1930s onward
All three waves began together in the 1980s with the rise of management schools
Human relations ~1900s, classical ~1930s, modern ~1950s onward
questions.why: ~1900s efficiency, ~1930s people, ~1950s systems and flexibility. See §2.2.

questions.stem: Identify Taylor's three ideas.
options: One best way, specialisation and training, pay linked to output
Clear rules, a defined hierarchy and written records of every decision
Attention, respect and inclusion for every worker on the floor
Plan the work, organise the people and lead by personal example
questions.why: Scientific management: better methods, trained specialists, incentives. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Identify the thinker who designed the fair, rule-based large organisation.
options: Max Weber
Frederick Taylor
Elton Mayo
Fayol
questions.why: Weber's bureaucracy: clear rules applied equally, hierarchy, merit. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Identify the thinker behind the Hawthorne studies.
options: Elton Mayo
Max Weber
Frederick Taylor
Henri Fayol
questions.why: Mayo's Hawthorne studies started the human relations movement. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Explain the phrase 'failures live between the boxes'.
options: Most problems happen in the hand-offs between departments, not inside one department
Failures are caused by the boxes on the organisation chart being drawn in the wrong order
Only the boxes at the top of the chart fail, because that is where the big decisions are made
Problems are always one person's fault, and the manager's job is to find out whose
questions.why: Systems thinking: trace the chain across departments instead of blaming the nearest person. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Describe what a systems manager does when something fails.
options: Traces the chain of connected causes and fixes the root
Blames the person nearest to the failure and makes an example of them
Ignores the failure until a customer complains and then offers a discount
Adds a new rule immediately so that the same failure cannot happen again
questions.why: Systems managers trace the chain. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Identify the chapter's airline example of the systems perspective.
options: One missed inspection grounded a plane, delayed four flights and lowered next month's bookings
A pilot who arrived late once and was dismissed to protect the airline's reputation
An airline that bought new planes and saw its maintenance costs fall the following year
A marketing campaign that failed because the advertising agency misunderstood the brief
questions.why: One technical failure travelled through connected parts into a marketing problem. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Identify the four things the right management style depends on.
options: The situation, the people, the environment and the organisation
The manager's mood, age, title and salary
Taylor's, Fayol's, Weber's and Mayo's ideas
Profit, cost, time and quality
questions.why: Contingency thinking: it depends on these four. See §2.7.

questions.stem: Explain when 'it depends' is a serious answer.
options: When you can say exactly what it depends on
When you do not want to make a decision and need more time to think
Never — managers must always have one clear rule for every situation
Only in creative companies, where there are no routine or safety-critical tasks
questions.why: Contingency: 'it depends' is serious if you name the factors. See §2.7.

questions.stem: Describe the contingency view of Taylor's and Mayo's ideas.
options: Both are tools; the manager picks the mix that fits the situation
Taylor was right and Mayo was wrong, because efficiency is what pays the wages
Mayo was right and Taylor was wrong, because people are more important than methods
Neither is useful today, because both were developed for factories a century ago
questions.why: The strongest answers are mixes chosen by reading the situation. See §2.7.

questions.stem: Describe how the chapter compares the 1910 manager with today's manager.
options: Different problems, not harder: waste and chaos then, complexity and speed now, with better tools
Today's manager has a much easier job, because computers handle the planning and the records
The 1910 manager had better tools, because the work was simpler and the workers obeyed
The problems are exactly the same, because people and organisations have not changed
questions.why: Different, not harder. See §2.8.

questions.stem: Identify what employees expect today that they did not expect in 1910.
options: Meaning, flexibility and to be heard
Only a fair wage paid on time at the end of the week
A lifetime job in one factory with a pension at the end
Strict supervision and clear instructions for every task
questions.why: New expectations are one of today's four challenges. See §2.8.

questions.stem: Explain how AI changes management, according to the chapter.
options: It is a new challenge managers must learn to use, like technology in every earlier era
It makes managers unnecessary, because the software can plan, organise and control
It has no real effect on management, because managing people has not changed
It only affects factories and warehouses, not offices, hospitals or schools
questions.why: AI is one of today's challenges, to be met with today's tools. See §2.8.

questions.stem: Analyse a start-up that grew from 5 friends to 120 employees and now has confusion, duplicate work and low motivation. Determine the chapter's explanation.
options: The same growth problems that produced the classical schools in 1910
The employees are lazy
The founders were bad people who did not care about the staff they hired
The product is wrong, so the employees have lost faith in the company's future
questions.why: Communication, coordination and motivation break when a firm grows. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Determine the problem that produced Fayol's and Weber's ideas.
options: Coordination — who does what in a large organisation
Lighting in the early factories
Customers wanting lower prices and better quality at the same time
Workers wanting shorter hours and better pay for the same output
questions.why: Fayol structured the organisation; Weber made it fair. See §2.1 and §2.4.

questions.stem: Determine the problem that produced Mayo's ideas.
options: Motivation — strangers in big firms did not care about the work
Communication by letter to the factory floor
Technology — machines were replacing skilled workers faster than they could be retrained
Taxation — governments were taxing factories more heavily each year
questions.why: Human relations answered the motivation problem. See §2.1 and §2.5.

questions.stem: Select the workplace where Taylor's standardisation fits best.
options: A fast-food kitchen
A design start-up inventing a new product
A university research team
A jazz band
questions.why: Routine, repeatable work is where the one best way wins. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Analyse a factory that standardised every task and now has bored workers and no new ideas. Determine the cause.
options: The known cost of scientific management: repetition kills morale and switches off the brain
The workers are not trained well enough to understand the reason behind each standard
The standards were too loose, so the workers lost confidence in the method
Pay was set too high, so the workers no longer had any incentive to suggest improvements
questions.why: Standardisation trades creativity and morale for speed. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Determine the Fayol principle broken when a nurse receives orders from three different managers.
options: Unity of command
Division of work
Scalar chain
Equity
questions.why: One boss per person. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Analyse a company that promotes the owner's nephew over a better-qualified employee. Determine what Weber would say.
options: Positions must be earned by merit, not family
That is normal in a bureaucracy, where the owner's authority is final
Family loyalty is more important than qualifications in a growing business
It depends on the nephew's age and how long he has worked in the firm
questions.why: Weber's bureaucracy replaced favouritism with merit. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Determine the lesson for a manager whose team improved while she was simply observing them with interest.
options: The Hawthorne effect — attention itself improves performance
Observation always makes people nervous, so the improvement must be a measurement error
The lights or working conditions must have changed at the same time without her noticing
The team was faking the improvement to impress her and will return to normal soon
questions.why: Productivity rose because someone paid attention. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Select the action that makes employees feel respected, supported and included.
options: Asking for their ideas and acting on one of them
A yearly pizza party to thank the whole team for its effort
A bigger bonus for the top seller at the end of each quarter
A stricter attendance rule applied equally to every employee
questions.why: Mayo's trio needs real attention, not treats. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Analyse a hospital where the lab, pharmacy and ward each did their job but the patient waited six hours. Determine the perspective that explains it.
options: Systems — the failure sits in the hand-offs between departments
Scientific management — the staff worked too slowly
Human relations — the staff were unhappy and did not care about the patient
Bureaucracy — too many forms had to be completed at each stage of the visit
questions.why: Everything is connected; failures live between the boxes. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Select the first action of a systems manager after a customer complaint.
options: Trace the chain of events across departments to find the cause
Punish the employee who served the customer so that the team learns the lesson
Offer the customer a discount and move on to the next problem
Write a new rule immediately so that the complaint cannot be repeated
questions.why: Trace the chain instead of blaming the nearest person. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Classify a manager who runs a team split between the office and home.
options: Facing the hybrid-work challenge
Facing a 1910 factory coordination problem
Using scientific management on knowledge workers
Using Weber's bureaucracy to control remote staff
questions.why: Hybrid work is one of today's four challenges. See §2.8.

questions.stem: Analyse a manager who says management today is impossible because of AI. Determine the chapter's response.
options: Every era solved its own problem with its own ideas and better tools — this one is different, not harder
Agree — AI changes so fast that no manager can plan, organise or control effectively any more
AI has nothing to do with management, so the manager should concentrate on people
Managers should ignore AI until the technology settles down and the rules are clear
questions.why: Different, not harder. See §2.8.

questions.stem: Select the modern challenge behind a Dubai firm managing teams in four countries.
options: Globalisation
Lighting in factories
Unity of command
Factory efficiency
questions.why: Globalisation is one of today's challenges. See §2.8.
